name: Activation-mass (expected value) plot
summary: A feature's activation histogram with each bin weighted by activation magnitude instead of counted once per token, so a bin's height is total activation contributed rather than number of firings. It answers where a feature's influence on the model comes from, not how often it fires.
explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

The claim on the table is [[activation-specificity]] for the [[arabic-script-feature]]: when this feature fires, the text is Arabic script. The paper has a number for it — 81% of the tokens the feature is active on score as Arabic under an independent [[computational-proxy]], against a 0.13% base rate — and a [[feature-activation-distribution-plot]]. Both count every firing once, the wrong weighting for the claim. A [[feature]] fires at 0.2 on some tokens and 7 on others, and in this one-layer model a feature's contribution to the logits is approximately linear in its activation ([[linear-logit-effects]]), so those firings do not matter equally, which the paper states as [[large-activations-dominate]].

That matters because the impure region is also the crowded one: about 25% Arabic where the feature is barely on, about 98% above activation 5. A count histogram is tallest exactly where the interpretation is weakest, and a plain average inherits that bias without showing it. A table of purity per band would give the percentages but not how much of the feature's output each band supplies. Multiplying each bin's count by its activation level is the smallest change that puts frequency and consequence in one picture. The paper calls the result an [[expected-value-plot]], borrowed from Cammarata et al.'s curve detector work. What it assumes rather than shows is that magnitude is the right currency: firm for one layer, the paper says, conjectural for deeper models.

### How to read it, step by step

Two of the three encodings are copied from the companion histogram — that is the trap. The horizontal axis is the same [[feature-activation]] level, the post-ReLU scalar the [[sparse-autoencoder]] assigns to this feature's direction on a token, running from just above zero to 9, exact zeros left out because the [[l1-sparsity-penalty]] makes them the overwhelming majority. The colour is the same split by the [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]] $\log(P(s\mid\text{Arabic Script})/P(s))$: deep blue at $-5$, white at $0$, deep red at $+5$, red stacked underneath, legend printed on the companion.

Only the vertical axis changed, and it is no longer a token count. A bin's height is how many tokens landed in it times how hard the feature fired on them: total activation contributed, in units (0K to 35K) set by the sample size. The bins are joined into a filled area rather than drawn as bars, but each x position is still one bin, and the total area is the feature's whole output.

Check the difference yourself, both charts open. At the far left the companion peaks above 5K tokens and is visibly blue; here the curve is on the floor, because a large count times an activation near zero is almost nothing. Near 6.9 the companion has a lower hump of about 4.7K, and $4.7\text{K}\times6.9\approx32\text{K}$ — this chart's peak. Then read blue as a fraction of a column's height, not as a width.

### What a bad result would look like

Mass piled at the left and decaying rightward: the influence coming from weak, impure firings, with the 98%-pure region doing almost none of the work. Or blue keeping a broad share of the area after weighting — non-Arabic strings driving the feature hard, [[polysemanticity]] surviving the test rather than being excluded by it. Or red filling every activation level, which would say the proxy calls most text Arabic, proving nothing. The figure shows mass concentrated between 5 and 8 and blue reduced to a hairline.

It does not adjudicate the [[weak-activation-hypotheses]]; it argues only that whichever is right, the tail carries little weight. It cannot separate proxy false negatives at high activation from genuine non-Arabic firing, and the weighting is a choice, not a neutral view.

### Where it comes back

As a drawn figure, once: fig-9, read against its companion. The DNA, base64 and Hebrew case studies get the unweighted spectrum only, the argument carried over rather than redrawn, so this evidence exists for one feature. The move itself returns twice. [[activation-interval-analysis]] scores each band of the spectrum separately, then leans on the same large-activations argument to discount the low bands. [[importance-scoring]] re-weights the other way, toward what random text would give, and there the correction makes features look worse, not better.
